content: To monitor the impact of introducing the rubella vaccine, it is essential to document the incidence of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) following vaccine implementation. This data helps assess the vaccine's effectiveness and identify areas requiring further strengthening. Additionally, collecting epidemiological data on CRS and its burden on the population is critical for informing immunization strategies, particularly addressing immunity gaps among adolescents and young adults. Reviewing CRS data alongside rubella surveillance data is vital to evaluate progress toward achieving or maintaining rubella elimination goals. This evaluation includes reviewing hospital records to identify missed cases by comparing reported CRS cases with all cases meeting the suspected CRS case definition. The proportion of suspected cases reported but not tested should also be identified. Data from these evaluations should be included in the National Verification Committee’s reports for measles, rubella, and CRS. Infants with CRS or congenital rubella infection (CRI) shed live rubella virus for extended periods (60% shed within the first four months of life) and are highly infectious. These infants should be considered infectious until two clinical specimens, collected one month apart after three months of age, test negative for rubella virus detection or isolation. Infection control procedures should be followed during this period. In hospitals, these infants should remain in isolation, and caregivers should adhere to universal precautions. Close contacts, including family members and friends involved in the care of these infants, should either be immune or vaccinated against rubella as per national policy. In areas where follow-up testing of confirmed CRS and CRI cases is not feasible, emphasis should be placed on ensuring that close contacts and healthcare workers are vaccinated against rubella. Pregnant women should not be exposed to infants with CRS or CRI; if exposed, they should be tested for rubella. Active community searches should be conducted to identify additional CRS cases and review the vaccination status of children in the locality. Unimmunized children or those without vaccination records should be vaccinated with measlesand rubella-containing vaccines according to national recommendations. Contact tracing among mothers of infants with CRS or CRI is recommended to identify the source of the rubella virus in the mother. Rubella, also known as German measles, is a mild viral illness that primarily affects children and young adults, causing low-grade fever and rash. However, infection during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, can lead to miscarriage, fetal death, stillbirth, or congenital malformations known as congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Rubella is a leading cause of vaccine-preventable birth defects. The risk of congenital infection and defects is highest during the first 12 weeks of gestation and decreases thereafter, with defects being rare if infection occurs after the 20th week of gestation. Common congenital defects caused by CRS include cataracts, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, and developmental delays. Infants with CRS often present with multiple defects but may also present with a single defect, most commonly hearing impairment. Globally, the number of reported CRS cases increased from 302 in 2012 to 603 in 2020, primarily due to the initiation of CRS surveillance and reporting in populous countries such as Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan. The number of countries in the WHO South-East Asia Region reporting CRS cases increased from two in 2002 to ten in 2016. North Korea, Sri Lanka, and Thailand report CRS cases as part of their national integrated disease surveillance programs. The South-East Asia Region bears the highest burden of CRS cases, with cases identified through sentinel site surveillance in eight countries. Bangladesh also utilizes population-based CRS surveillance. CRS is associated with significant morbidity and mortality, with estimated mortality rates ranging from 20–40%. Infants born with cardiac defects have the highest risk of mortality. The estimated mean incidence rate of CRS in the region since 2010 has been 121 per 100,000 live births, translating to approximately 49,229 annual cases. The regional goal is to achieve measles and rubella elimination by 2023. Rubella elimination in two countries of the region is estimated to have prevented 52,118 CRS cases annually. In 2020, the Maldives and Sri Lanka were verified to have eliminated rubella and sustained their elimination status in 2021. Facility-based surveillance for CRS in India revealed that about one-fifth of suspected CRS patients during 2016–2018 had laboratory-confirmed rubella infection, indicating continued rubella transmission in the country. The estimated incidence of CRS in India varies depending on the model used, with approximately 14,520–50,028 infants affected annually. The rubella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine that provides more than 95% long-lasting immunity with a single dose, likely offering lifelong protection. It is available in monovalent formulations or in combination with other vaccines, such as measles (MR), measles and mumps (MMR), or measles, mumps, and varicella (MMRV). To establish a CRS surveillance system, national coordinators for epidemiology and laboratories are necessary to manage the system's components. Sentinel sites should be identified where infants with common CRS-associated defects, such as cataracts, heart defects, or deafness, are likely to be evaluated and treated. Surveillance activities should be initiated once coordinators and participating sites are identified, and providers are trained in standard operating procedures (SOPs) for CRS surveillance. Data should be analyzed annually or more frequently if necessary, and feedback should be provided to stakeholders to improve the system. Only individuals immune to rubella should have contact with affected infants. In hospitals, these infants should be isolated, and caregivers should wear protective gowns and gloves and be immunized against rubella.
